body:
Where did the Kushans come from?

The Kushans were a ruling group of Central Asian origin associated with the larger Yuezhi confederation. The Yuezhi moved westwards from regions near northwestern China and eventually reached Bactria, in and around present-day northern Afghanistan and adjoining Central Asian territories.

One branch of the Yuezhi developed into the Kushan ruling house. Kujula Kadphises is remembered as an important early Kushan ruler who united groups under his authority and helped establish Kushan power.

The Kushans later extended their rule south of the Hindu Kush into northwestern India. Their empire became especially influential during the 1st to 3rd centuries CE.

The Kushans, Shakas and Indo-Greeks must be understood as distinct political and cultural groups. They came from different backgrounds, even though they governed some of the same regions at different times and interacted with the communities living there.

Important Kushan political centres

The Kushan Empire linked Central Asian territories with major cities in northwestern and northern India. Its two especially important political centres under Kanishka were:

  • Purushapura: the ancient name of Peshawar, now in Pakistan. It was an important northwestern royal centre.
  • Mathura: located in present-day Uttar Pradesh. It was another major centre of Kushan political and cultural activity.

Taxila, in present-day Pakistan, was also an important city within the Kushan sphere. It should be remembered as a significant centre, but not confused with the two principal centres named above.

Purushapura = Peshawar. The two major Kushan centres commonly associated with Kanishka are Peshawar and Mathura. Taxila was another important city.

The Silk Route and the Kushan Empire

The Silk Route was a network of long-distance trade routes connecting China, Central Asia and lands farther west. It was not one continuous road. Different branches connected inland trading centres with other land routes and seaports.

Silk produced in China was transported westwards through Central Asia. Traders carried goods across mountains and deserts using pack animals. Along these routes, merchants exchanged not only silk but also other valuable commodities.

The Kushans controlled important parts of the network linking Central Asia with northwestern India. One route connected Central Asia with ports near the mouth of the Indus River, from where goods could enter maritime trading networks extending westwards towards the Roman world.

Control of trade routes benefited rulers because they could receive taxes, tribute and payments associated with commercial movement. In return, rulers had an interest in protecting merchants and maintaining access to markets.

Kushan gold coins

The Kushans were among the earliest rulers in the Indian subcontinent to issue gold coins on a substantial scale. Kushan gold coinage became important during the early centuries CE and was associated with extensive commercial activity.

This fact must be distinguished from the better-known feature of Indo-Greek coinage. The Indo-Greeks are especially associated with early coins bearing the names and portraits of rulers, whereas the Kushans are particularly associated with early and extensive gold coinage.

Wider consequences of Kushan connections

The empire connected areas in which different languages, religious traditions and artistic practices already existed. Its territories included important Buddhist centres and communities with Iranian, Greek and Indian cultural influences.

Trade routes also provided channels for the movement of Buddhist monks, religious ideas and artistic traditions between India and Central Asia. These exchanges help explain why the Kushan period is important not only for political history but also for the wider spread of Buddhism.

Prelims focus

  • The Kushans were associated with the Yuezhi of Central Asian origin.
  • Kujula Kadphises was an important early Kushan ruler.
  • Purushapura is the ancient name of Peshawar.
  • Peshawar and Mathura were major Kushan political centres.
  • Kushan power linked Central Asian land trade with northwestern Indian routes and Indus ports.
  • Trap: The Indo-Greeks are noted for early named and portrait coins; the Kushans are noted for extensive early gold coinage.

[NCERT, Our Pasts-I, Class 6, Chapter 10: Traders, Kings and Pilgrims, printed pp. 101–103; NCERT, Themes in Indian History, Part I, Class 12, Theme 2, printed pp. 44–45; Metropolitan Museum of Art, Department of Asian Art, Kushan Empire (ca. Second Century B.C.–Third Century A.D.), Heilbrunn Timeline of Art History, October 2000, consulted 19 November 2026.]

title: The Kushans: Central Asian Origins, Capitals and Trade Routes

body:
Kanishka as a Kushan ruler

Kanishka I was one of the most prominent rulers of the Kushan Empire. He is generally placed in the 2nd century CE and is especially remembered for his association with Buddhism and the cultural development of northern India and Central Asia.

His two major political centres were Purushapura (Peshawar) and Mathura. These centres connected the Kushan administration with the northwestern routes and the major settlements of northern India.

Kanishka and the Buddhist council

According to northern Buddhist traditions, Kanishka convened an important Buddhist council, commonly called the Fourth Buddhist Council.

The council is traditionally associated with Kashmir, frequently identified with Kundalavana. Vasumitra is traditionally named as an important leader or presiding scholar. The gathering is especially associated with the Sarvastivada Buddhist school and the discussion or explanation of Buddhist teachings.

A Buddhist council was an assembly of monks and scholars who discussed questions of doctrine and discipline. In the tradition associated with Kanishka, the emphasis was particularly on the interpretation and organisation of Buddhist learning.

The designation Fourth Buddhist Council is not identical across all Buddhist traditions. Northern Buddhist accounts associate such a council with Kanishka in Kashmir, while Theravada traditions preserve a different account of a fourth council in Sri Lanka. Therefore, Kashmir, Vasumitra and Kanishka should be presented as associations preserved in northern Buddhist tradition.

Ashvaghosha and the Buddhacharita

Ashvaghosha was a Buddhist poet and scholar traditionally associated with Kanishka's court. He is best known for the Buddhacharita, a Sanskrit poetic account of the life of the Buddha.

The important distinction is between the ruler and the author: Kanishka is associated with the patronage of Buddhist learning, while Ashvaghosha is associated with the composition of the Buddhacharita.

Mahayana Buddhism during the Kushan period

The early centuries CE witnessed important developments in Mahayana Buddhism. The word Mahayana means great vehicle. Mahayana traditions placed particular emphasis on the ideal of the Bodhisattva, who seeks Buddhahood for the benefit of other beings.

In this religious ideal, compassion and assistance to others are central. Bodhisattvas are represented as beings committed to enlightenment and the welfare of others rather than seeking liberation solely for themselves.

During the same broad period, the production and worship of images of the Buddha became increasingly important. Mathura and Gandhara, including Taxila, became major centres associated with Buddhist images.

The Kushan territories and connected trade routes helped Buddhist ideas move across Central Asia towards China, from where Buddhism later spread into other parts of East Asia.

Kanishka's council and the development of Mahayana Buddhism are related features of the broad period, but they are not the same event. It is misleading to claim that the Kashmir council definitely founded Mahayana Buddhism.

Why Kanishka's date needs care

The Shaka era begins in 78 CE, but identifying 78 CE as Kanishka's accession date is not secure. Some older textbook chronologies made that association. A widely supported modern reconstruction instead places the beginning of an era associated with Kanishka around 127 CE.

Even this reconstructed era date should not automatically be treated as the proven first year of Kanishka's reign. For ordinary prelims study, the stable distinction is that 78 CE marks the beginning of the Shaka era, while Kanishka's exact accession date remains uncertain.

Prelims focus

  • Kanishka I was a prominent Kushan ruler of the early centuries CE.
  • His major centres were Purushapura/Peshawar and Mathura.
  • Northern Buddhist traditions associate him with the Fourth Buddhist Council in Kashmir.
  • Vasumitra and the Sarvastivada school are associated with that council.
  • Ashvaghosha is associated with the Sanskrit work Buddhacharita.
  • Trap: The Shaka era began in 78 CE; Kanishka's exact accession date is not securely established.

[NCERT, Our Pasts-I, Class 6, Chapter 10: Traders, Kings and Pilgrims, printed pp. 102–104; NCERT, Themes in Indian History, Part I, Class 12, Theme 2, printed p. 50, including the qualification on Kanishka's accession; Encyclopaedia Iranica, Kushan Dynasty III: Chronology of the Kushans, section on the era of Kanishka, consulted 19 November 2026; Encyclopedia of Buddhism, Buddhist Councils, section Fourth Council in Kashmir, consulted 19 November 2026.]

pictures.alt: Northern Buddhist tradition links Kanishka’s council with Kashmir, Vasumitra and Sarvastivada; fourth-council identifications vary across traditions.
pictures.caption: The traditional associations of Kanishka's Buddhist council.

title: Kanishka, the Buddhist Council and Mahayana Buddhism

body:
Why Central Asian contacts influenced Indian culture

From Alexander's campaign to the Kushan period, northwestern India remained connected with the regions beyond the Hindu Kush. Different rulers arrived from the west or northwest, but each governed territories in which Indian communities and existing religious traditions were already present.

These contacts encouraged exchanges involving political practices, languages, coinage, trade and Buddhist art. The clearest artistic examples for this period are the centres of Gandhara and Mathura, both of which became important during the Kushan age.

Gandhara: Buddhist subjects and Hellenistic features

Gandhara was a historical region in the northwest, covering areas of present-day Pakistan and adjoining Afghanistan. Important centres included areas around Taxila and Peshawar.

Gandhara sculpture combined Buddhist subjects with artistic features influenced by several traditions, including Greek, Roman, Bactrian, Parthian and local styles.

Characteristic features of many Gandharan Buddha images include:

  • Carefully modelled facial and bodily features.
  • Wavy or curly hair.
  • Robes with prominent, realistically carved folds.
  • A style of drapery and bodily representation showing Hellenistic and Greco-Roman influence.

These features do not make the sculptures Greek religious images. They are Buddhist works made in a region with a long history of cultural interaction.

Mathura: An important indigenous sculptural tradition

Mathura, in present-day Uttar Pradesh, developed a powerful local sculptural tradition. During the Kushan period, it became a major centre for images of the Buddha as well as Jain and Brahmanical subjects.

The earliest Mathura Buddha images drew upon earlier Indian Yaksha sculptural traditions. Typical features of many Kushan-period images include:

  • Use of reddish or mottled sandstone.
  • Fuller, rounded bodily forms and broad shoulders.
  • More visibly indigenous Indian sculptural conventions.
  • A comparatively simple treatment of the robe in several early examples.

The important distinction is that Gandhara is especially noted for its Hellenistic-influenced features, while Mathura developed strongly from existing Indian sculptural traditions. Both produced Buddhist images during the Kushan period.

These are characteristic tendencies, not rules that apply to every surviving sculpture. Gandhara and Mathura were both centres of Buddhist image-making, and they should not be classified as exclusively foreign or exclusively Buddhist in every aspect of their artistic production.

One-glance chronology

The principal phases of foreign contact did not form one simple succession of completely separate empires. Their political territories and dates sometimes overlapped.

  • 327–325 BCE: Alexander's campaign in northwestern India; Battle of Hydaspes in 326 BCE.
  • 2nd–1st centuries BCE: Indo-Greek kingdoms in northwestern India; Menander is an important ruler.
  • From about the 1st century BCE: Shaka political activity in northwestern and western India.
  • 1st–3rd centuries CE: Major period of Kushan power and Central Asian trade connections.
  • 78 CE: Beginning of the Shaka era, not a securely established accession date for Kanishka.
  • 2nd century CE: Kanishka's reign broadly belongs to this period; Rudradaman's Junagadh inscription dates to approximately 150–151 CE.

Putting the distinctions together

Alexander is associated with a short military campaign and the Battle of Hydaspes. The Indo-Greeks are associated with Hellenistic rule, Menander and bilingual coins. The Shakas are associated with Central Asian origins, Western Kshatrapa rule and Rudradaman's inscription in Gujarat. The Kushans are associated with Yuezhi origins, Peshawar and Mathura, gold coinage, Silk Route connections and Kanishka's Buddhist patronage.

Understanding these differences is more reliable than treating every foreign-origin ruler in ancient northwestern India as belonging to the same dynasty.

Prelims focus

  • Gandhara art developed in the northwest and shows Hellenistic-influenced features.
  • Mathura art developed from local Indian sculptural traditions and was important under the Kushans.
  • Both Gandhara and Mathura produced Buddha images during the Kushan period.
  • Alexander's campaign preceded the Indo-Greek kingdoms by more than a century.
  • Indo-Greek, Shaka and Kushan political histories overlapped in parts of northwestern India.
  • Trap: The presence of Greek artistic influence in Gandhara does not mean that all Kushan art was Greek in origin.

[NCERT, An Introduction to Indian Art, Part I, Class 11, Chapter 4: Post-Mauryan Trends in Indian Art and Architecture, printed pp. 30–31 and 48–51; NCERT, Themes in Indian History, Part I, Class 12, Theme 2: Kings, Farmers and Towns, printed pp. 35–36 and 44–50; NCERT, Our Pasts-I, Class 6, Chapter 10: Traders, Kings and Pilgrims, printed pp. 102–104; Metropolitan Museum of Art, Department of Asian Art, Kushan Empire, section on Gandhara and Buddhist imagery, consulted 19 November 2026.]
